```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
set.seed(258)

# ---- Colours ---------------------------------------------------------------
col_null  <- "#1f4e79"   # null distribution (blue)
col_alt   <- "#c62828"   # alternative distribution (red)
fill_pow  <- "rgba(46,125,50,0.35)"   # power region (green)
line_pow  <- "rgba(46,125,50,0.9)"
fill_a    <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.55)"  # Type I / alpha (orange)
line_a    <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)"
fill_b    <- "rgba(198,40,40,0.20)"   # Type II / beta (red wash)
line_b    <- "rgba(198,40,40,0.6)"

# ---- Overlap of H0 and Ha distributions; shade the power region ------------
power_overlap <- function(mu0, mua, se0, sea = se0, alpha = 0.05,
                          alternative = "greater", title = "",
                          xlab = "sample mean", show_beta = FALSE,
                          cutoff_label = NULL, power_label = NULL,
                          beta_label = NULL,
                          width = 640, height = 255) {
  zc    <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
  xcrit <- if (alternative == "less") mu0 - zc * se0 else mu0 + zc * se0
  s     <- if (alternative == "less") -1 else 1
  lo <- min(mu0 - 4 * se0, mua - 4 * sea)
  hi <- max(mu0 + 4 * se0, mua + 4 * sea)
  x  <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 600)
  y0 <- dnorm(x, mu0, se0)
  ya <- dnorm(x, mua, sea)
  keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= xcrit else x >= xcrit
  ymax <- max(c(y0, ya))
  p <- plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y0, line = list(color = col_null, width = 3),
              name = "H₀", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = ya, line = list(color = col_alt, width = 3),
              name = "Hₐ", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_trace(x = x[keep], y = ya[keep], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_pow,
              line = list(color = line_pow, width = 1),
              name = "Power", hoverinfo = "x+y")
  if (show_beta) {
    bk <- !keep
    p <- p |>
      add_trace(x = x[bk], y = ya[bk], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
                fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_b,
                line = list(color = line_b, width = 1),
                name = "β", hoverinfo = "x+y")
  }
  has_lab <- !is.null(power_label) || !is.null(beta_label)
  bmar <- if (has_lab) 100 else 34
  p |> layout(
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
    xaxis = list(title = list(text = xlab, standoff = if (has_lab) 48 else 0),
                 zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                 range = c(0, ymax * 1.28), fixedrange = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 28, r = 12, t = 38, b = bmar),
    showlegend = FALSE, hovermode = "x unified",
    shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = xcrit, x1 = xcrit,
                       y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.16,
                       line = list(color = "#333", width = 2, dash = "dash"))),
    annotations = c(
      list(
        list(x = mu0, y = max(y0) * 1.07, text = "H₀",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_null, size = 14)),
        list(x = mua, y = max(ya) * 1.07, text = "Hₐ",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_alt, size = 14)),
        list(x = xcrit, y = ymax * 1.16,
             text = if (!is.null(cutoff_label)) cutoff_label else "cutoff",
             showarrow = FALSE, yanchor = "bottom",
             font = list(color = "#333", size = 11))),
      # power & β labels sit BELOW the plot with arrows pointing up
      if (!is.null(beta_label)) list(list(
        x = xcrit - s * 0.5 * se0, y = 0.05, text = beta_label,
        showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 40, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
        arrowcolor = "#c62828", font = list(color = "#c62828", size = 12))),
      if (!is.null(power_label)) list(list(
        x = mua, y = 0.06, text = power_label,
        showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 40, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
        arrowcolor = line_pow, font = list(color = "#1b5e20", size = 12)))
    )
  ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Type I (alpha) and Type II (beta) error regions -----------------------
error_plot <- function(mu0, mua, se, alpha = 0.05, alternative = "greater",
                       title = "Type I (α) and Type II (β)",
                       width = 640, height = 260) {
  zc    <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
  xcrit <- if (alternative == "less") mu0 - zc * se else mu0 + zc * se
  lo <- min(mu0, mua) - 4 * se
  hi <- max(mu0, mua) + 4 * se
  x  <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 600)
  y0 <- dnorm(x, mu0, se)
  ya <- dnorm(x, mua, se)
  rej  <- if (alternative == "less") x <= xcrit else x >= xcrit
  ymax <- max(c(y0, ya))
  s <- if (alternative == "less") -1 else 1
  hy <- 0.06                             # arrow-head height inside each sliver
  ax_x <- xcrit + s * 0.40 * se          # α: null sliver on the reject side
  bx_x <- xcrit - s * 0.45 * se          # β: alt sliver on the keep side
  pw_x <- mua                            # power: deep in the green region
  plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y0, line = list(color = col_null, width = 3),
              name = "H₀", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = ya, line = list(color = col_alt, width = 3),
              name = "Hₐ", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_trace(x = x[rej], y = ya[rej], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_pow,
              line = list(color = line_pow, width = 1),
              name = "power", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_trace(x = x[rej], y = y0[rej], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_a,
              line = list(color = line_a, width = 1),
              name = "α (Type I)", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_trace(x = x[!rej], y = ya[!rej], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_b,
              line = list(color = line_b, width = 1),
              name = "β (Type II)", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.28), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 28, r = 12, t = 38, b = 76),
      showlegend = FALSE, hovermode = "x unified",
      shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = xcrit, x1 = xcrit,
                         y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.06,
                         line = list(color = "#333", width = 2, dash = "dash"))),
      annotations = list(
        list(x = mu0, y = max(y0) * 1.07, text = "H₀ true",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_null, size = 11)),
        list(x = mua, y = max(ya) * 1.07, text = "Hₐ true",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_alt, size = 11)),
        # labels sit BELOW the curves; arrows point up into each region
        list(x = bx_x, y = hy, text = "β (Type II)",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = -24, ay = 40,
             arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.5, arrowcolor = "#c62828",
             font = list(color = "#c62828", size = 13)),
        list(x = ax_x, y = hy, text = "α (Type I)",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 22, ay = 64,
             arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.5, arrowcolor = "#b26a00",
             font = list(color = "#b26a00", size = 13)),
        list(x = pw_x, y = hy, text = "power",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 40,
             arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.5, arrowcolor = "#2e7d32",
             font = list(color = "#1b5e20", size = 13)))
    ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Power curve: power as a function of the true mean ----------------------
power_curve <- function(mu0, se, alpha = 0.05, alternative = "greater",
                        mu_lo, mu_hi, marks = NULL, title = "Power curve",
                        width = 640, height = 270) {
  zc  <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
  mus <- seq(mu_lo, mu_hi, length.out = 250)
  if (alternative == "less") {
    xcrit <- mu0 - zc * se
    pw <- pnorm((xcrit - mus) / se)
  } else {
    xcrit <- mu0 + zc * se
    pw <- pnorm((mus - xcrit) / se)
  }
  p <- plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = mus, y = pw,
              line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 4, dash = "dash"),
              name = "power", hoverinfo = "x+y")
  if (!is.null(marks)) {
    mp <- if (alternative == "less") pnorm((xcrit - marks) / se) else
                                      pnorm((marks - xcrit) / se)
    p <- p |> add_markers(x = marks, y = mp,
                          marker = list(color = "#f9a825", size = 11,
                                        line = list(color = "#b26a00", width = 1)),
                          hoverinfo = "x+y", name = "")
  }
  p |> layout(
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
    xaxis = list(title = "true mean μ", fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(title = "power", range = c(0, 1.03), fixedrange = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 46, r = 12, t = 38, b = 40), showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest"
  ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Proportion power as sample size grows ---------------------------------
prop_power_n <- function(p0, pa, alpha = 0.05, alternative = "less",
                         n_lo = 20, n_hi = 400, marks = NULL,
                         title = "Power rises with sample size",
                         width = 640, height = 270) {
  zc <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
  ns <- seq(n_lo, n_hi, by = 2)
  powfun <- function(n) {
    se0 <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
    sea <- sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / n)
    pcrit <- if (alternative == "less") p0 - zc * se0 else p0 + zc * se0
    if (alternative == "less") pnorm((pcrit - pa) / sea) else
                                pnorm((pa - pcrit) / sea)
  }
  pw <- vapply(ns, powfun, numeric(1))
  p <- plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = ns, y = pw,
              line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 4),
              name = "power", hoverinfo = "x+y")
  if (!is.null(marks)) {
    mp <- vapply(marks, powfun, numeric(1))
    p <- p |> add_markers(x = marks, y = mp,
                          marker = list(color = "#f9a825", size = 11,
                                        line = list(color = "#b26a00", width = 1)),
                          hoverinfo = "x+y", name = "")
  }
  p |> layout(
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
    xaxis = list(title = "sample size n", fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(title = "power", range = c(0, 1.03), fixedrange = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 46, r = 12, t = 38, b = 40), showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode = "closest"
  ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Simple one-tailed rejection-region sketch -----------------------------
tail_plot <- function(stat = 1.645, alternative = "greater",
                      title = "Rejection region", width = 620, height = 230) {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)
  y <- dnorm(x)
  keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= stat else x >= stat
  plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = col_null, width = 4),
              name = "N(0,1)", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    add_trace(x = x[keep], y = y[keep], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_a,
              line = list(color = line_a, width = 1),
              name = "reject", hoverinfo = "x+y") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE, range = c(-4, 4), fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 30, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28),
      showlegend = FALSE, hovermode = "x unified",
      annotations = list(list(x = stat, y = dnorm(stat) + 0.05,
        text = paste0("z = ", formatC(stat, format = "f", digits = 3)),
        showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#333", size = 11)))
    ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Interactive: dropdown to switch the sample size (or any case) ----------
# Builds one H0 line + one Ha line + one power-fill per case and wires a
# plotly dropdown that toggles which case is visible and updates the title
# and y-axis range to match. Runs fully client-side (no webR needed).
explore_power_n <- function(mu0, mua, sigma, ns, alpha = 0.05,
                            alternative = "less", xlab = "sample mean  x̄",
                            width = 760, height = 320) {
  zc  <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
  ses <- sigma / sqrt(ns)
  lo  <- min(mu0, mua) - 4 * max(ses)
  hi  <- max(mu0, mua) + 4 * max(ses)
  x   <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 600)
  powers <- numeric(length(ns))
  ymax   <- numeric(length(ns))
  p <- plot_ly(width = width, height = height)
  for (i in seq_along(ns)) {
    se    <- ses[i]
    xcrit <- if (alternative == "less") mu0 - zc * se else mu0 + zc * se
    y0    <- dnorm(x, mu0, se)
    ya    <- dnorm(x, mua, se)
    keep  <- if (alternative == "less") x <= xcrit else x >= xcrit
    powers[i] <- if (alternative == "less") pnorm((xcrit - mua) / se) else
                                            pnorm((mua - xcrit) / se)
    ymax[i]   <- dnorm(mu0, mu0, se)
    vis <- (i == 1)
    p <- p |>
      add_lines(x = x, y = y0, visible = vis,
                line = list(color = col_null, width = 3),
                name = "H₀", hoverinfo = "none") |>
      add_lines(x = x, y = ya, visible = vis,
                line = list(color = col_alt, width = 3),
                name = "Hₐ", hoverinfo = "none") |>
      add_trace(x = x[keep], y = ya[keep], visible = vis, type = "scatter",
                mode = "lines", fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_pow,
                line = list(color = line_pow, width = 1),
                name = "power", hoverinfo = "none")
  }
  ttl <- function(i) paste0("n = ", ns[i], "   →   power = ",
                            formatC(powers[i], format = "f", digits = 3))
  buttons <- lapply(seq_along(ns), function(i) {
    v <- rep(FALSE, 3 * length(ns))
    v[((i - 1) * 3 + 1):((i - 1) * 3 + 3)] <- TRUE
    list(method = "update", label = paste0("n = ", ns[i]),
         args = list(list(visible = v),
                     list("title.text"  = ttl(i),
                          "yaxis.range"  = c(0, ymax[i] * 1.22))))
  })
  p |> layout(
    title = list(text = ttl(1), x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
    xaxis = list(title = xlab, zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                 range = c(0, ymax[1] * 1.22), fixedrange = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 28, r = 12, t = 74, b = 40), showlegend = FALSE,
    updatemenus = list(list(type = "dropdown", direction = "down",
                            x = 0.99, xanchor = "right", y = 1.22,
                            yanchor = "top", pad = list(t = 2, r = 2),
                            font = list(size = 12), buttons = buttons)),
    annotations = list(list(x = 0.99, y = 1.30, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
                            xanchor = "right", showarrow = FALSE,
                            text = "choose sample size",
                            font = list(size = 11, color = "#667174")))
  ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# ---- Two-sided test: both rejection tails, all regions shaded ---------------
power_two_sided <- function(mu0, mua, se, alpha = 0.05,
                            xlab = "sample mean  x̄",
                            width = 880, height = 330) {
  zc <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
  c1 <- mu0 - zc * se
  c2 <- mu0 + zc * se
  lo <- min(mu0, mua) - 4 * se
  hi <- max(mu0, mua) + 4 * se
  x  <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 800)
  y0 <- dnorm(x, mu0, se)
  ya <- dnorm(x, mua, se)
  L <- x <= c1
  R <- x >= c2
  M <- x >= c1 & x <= c2
  ymax <- max(c(y0, ya))
  plot_ly(width = width, height = height) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y0, line = list(color = col_null, width = 3),
              name = "H₀", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = ya, line = list(color = col_alt, width = 3),
              name = "Hₐ", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[L], y = ya[L], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_pow,
              line = list(color = line_pow, width = 1),
              name = "power (left)", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[R], y = ya[R], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_pow,
              line = list(color = line_pow, width = 1),
              name = "power (right)", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[M], y = ya[M], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_b,
              line = list(color = line_b, width = 1),
              name = "β", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[L], y = y0[L], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_a,
              line = list(color = line_a, width = 1),
              name = "α/2", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[R], y = y0[R], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_a,
              line = list(color = line_a, width = 1),
              name = "α/2", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      xaxis = list(title = xlab, zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.30), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 28, r = 12, t = 30, b = 88),
      showlegend = FALSE, hovermode = FALSE,
      shapes = list(
        list(type = "line", x0 = c1, x1 = c1, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.12,
             line = list(color = "#333", width = 2, dash = "dash")),
        list(type = "line", x0 = c2, x1 = c2, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.12,
             line = list(color = "#333", width = 2, dash = "dash"))),
      annotations = list(
        list(x = mu0, y = max(y0) * 1.07, text = "H₀",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_null, size = 14)),
        list(x = mua, y = max(ya) * 1.07, text = "Hₐ",
             showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = col_alt, size = 14)),
        list(x = c1, y = ymax * 1.12, text = paste0("cutoff = ", round(c1, 2)),
             showarrow = FALSE, yanchor = "bottom",
             font = list(color = "#333", size = 11)),
        list(x = c2, y = ymax * 1.12, text = paste0("cutoff = ", round(c2, 2)),
             showarrow = FALSE, yanchor = "bottom",
             font = list(color = "#333", size = 11)),
        list(x = c1 - 0.45 * se, y = 0.05, text = "α/2",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 38, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
             arrowcolor = line_a, font = list(color = "#b28704", size = 12)),
        list(x = c2 + 0.45 * se, y = 0.05, text = "α/2",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 38, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
             arrowcolor = line_a, font = list(color = "#b28704", size = 12)),
        list(x = c2 - 0.6 * se, y = 0.05, text = "β",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 38, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
             arrowcolor = "#c62828", font = list(color = "#c62828", size = 12)),
        list(x = mua + 1.2 * se, y = 0.06, text = "power",
             showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = 38, arrowhead = 2, arrowwidth = 1.3,
             arrowcolor = line_pow, font = list(color = "#1b5e20", size = 12)))
    ) |> config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}
```

# Chapter 7: Statistical Power {.title-slide}

<style>
:root {
  --sta-teal: #00695c;
  --sta-teal-dark: #004d40;
  --sta-teal-light: #e0f2f1;
  --sta-blue: #c8e6f3;
  --sta-blue-soft: #eef8fb;
  --sta-grey: #f5f6f7;
  --sta-yellow: #fff8e1;
  --sta-orange: #f9a825;
  --sta-text: #2f3437;
  --sta-muted: #667174;
  --sta-border: #d8dee2;
  --sta-code: #f3f4f5;
}
.reveal { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: var(--sta-text); }
.reveal .slides section { text-align: left; padding: 18px 30px; box-sizing: border-box; }
.reveal h1, .reveal h2, .reveal h3 { color: var(--sta-text); line-height: 1.08; }
.reveal h1 { font-size: 1.72em !important; }
.reveal h2 {
  font-size: 1.48em !important;
  border-bottom: 3px solid var(--sta-teal);
  padding-bottom: 4px;
  margin-bottom: 12px;
}
.reveal h3 { font-size: 1.02em !important; margin-bottom: 0.2em; }
.reveal p, .reveal li { font-size: 0.74em; line-height: 1.3; }
.title-slide { text-align: center !important; }
.title-slide h1 { font-size: 1.72em !important; margin-top: 0.4em; }
.title-slide h2 { font-size: 1.6em !important; border-bottom: none !important; margin-top: 0.6em; text-align: center; }
.title-slide p { font-size: 0.78em; color: var(--sta-muted); }
.two-col, .two-col-wide, .three-col, .four-grid, .procedure-grid, .decision-grid, .slide-stack {
  display: grid;
  gap: 24px;
  align-items: start;
}
.two-col { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
.two-col-wide { grid-template-columns: 1.12fr 0.88fr; }
.three-col { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
.four-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); }
.procedure-grid { grid-template-columns: 0.78fr 1.22fr; }

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}

<span class="label">7.1 - Power</span>
What power means, and the four things that push it up or down.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">7.2 - Errors</span>
Type I ($\alpha$) and Type II ($\beta$), and how power $=1-\beta$.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">7.3 - Planning</span>
Use a target power to choose the smallest sample size.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core skill</span>
Compute power against a specific alternative value.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core tool</span>
Use `pnorm()` and `qnorm()` for cutoffs, power, and sample size.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core habit</span>
A test is only useful if it can detect a real effect.
:::
::::

---

## 7.1 What Is Statistical Power?

::: {.defbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Definition 7.1</span>
The probability that a fixed-level significance test will reject $H_0$ when a particular **alternative** value of the parameter is true is called the **power** of the test against that alternative.

$$\text{Power}=P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ false}), \qquad 0<\text{power}<1$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">High power (near 1)</span>
The test is good at detecting effects that are really there.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Low power (near 0)</span>
The test is unreliable, it usually fails to reject even when $H_0$ is false.
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

The **power** of a hypothesis test is the probability that the test will:
::::

- Reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is actually true
- [Reject $H_0$ when $H_a$ is actually true]{.correct data-explanation="Power is the probability of correctly rejecting H₀ when the alternative is true: Power = 1 − β. Rejecting H₀ when it is true is the Type I error, with probability α."}
- Fail to reject $H_0$ when $H_a$ is true
- Fail to reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true

---

## What Affects Power?

:::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label" style="display:inline">Effect size</span> &nbsp;-&nbsp; Larger gaps between reality and $H_0$ are easier to detect $\Rightarrow$ more power.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label" style="display:inline">Sample size $n$</span> &nbsp;-&nbsp; Larger samples shrink the standard error $\Rightarrow$ more power.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label" style="display:inline">Significance level $\alpha$</span> &nbsp;-&nbsp; A larger $\alpha$ makes $H_0$ easier to reject $\Rightarrow$ more power (but more Type I risk).
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label" style="display:inline">Variability $\sigma$</span> &nbsp;-&nbsp; Less spread in the data $\Rightarrow$ narrower sampling distribution $\Rightarrow$ more power.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
You control $n$ and $\alpha$. The effect size and $\sigma$ are determined by the nature of the problem, so sample size is your main planning lever.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

Holding the effect size, $\sigma$, and $n$ fixed, you raise the significance level from $\alpha=0.01$ to $\alpha=0.05$. What happens to the power?
::::

- Power decreases
- [Power increases]{.correct data-explanation="A larger α enlarges the rejection region, so the test rejects H₀ more readily — including when Hₐ is true — which raises power. The trade-off is a higher Type I error rate."}
- Power is unchanged
- Power always becomes exactly 1

---

## 7.2 Type I and Type II Errors

::: {.notebox}
A hypothesis test can reach the **wrong** conclusion in two ways.
:::

::: {.tbl-center}
| | $H_0$ True | $H_0$ False |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Reject $H_0$** | [Type I ($\alpha$)]{.nw} | [Correct (power)]{.nw} |
| **Fail to reject $H_0$** | Correct | [Type II ($\beta$)]{.nw} |
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Type I error ($\alpha$)</span>
Reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is **true**.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Type II error ($\beta$)</span>
Fail to reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is **false**.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
A Type I error is usually treated as the more serious mistake, which is why we fix $\alpha$ in advance (often $0.05$).
:::

---

## Power Connects to the Errors

::: {.defbox}
The power of a test against an alternative is **1 minus** the Type II error probability for that alternative:

$$\text{Power}=1-\beta = 1 - P(\text{Type II})$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reading the picture</span>
The orange tail under $H_0$ is $\alpha$. The red region under $H_a$ is $\beta$. Everything else under $H_a$ is the **power**.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
error_plot(mu0 = 0, mua = 1.1, se = 1 / sqrt(10),
           alpha = 0.05, alternative = "greater",
           title = "α under H₀; β + power under Hₐ")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A test fails to reject $H_0$, but in reality $H_0$ is false. Which error has occurred?
::::

- Type I error
- [Type II error]{.correct data-explanation="Failing to reject a false H0 is a Type II error (probability β). Power = 1 − β is the chance we would have correctly rejected."}
- No error, we were cautious
- Both Type I and Type II

---

## Computing Power: The Recipe

::: {.slide-stack}
<ol class="step-list">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>1. Rejection rule in terms of the estimate.</strong> Convert the critical $z$ (or $z_\alpha$) into a cutoff $\bar{x}_*$ on the data scale using the null distribution.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>2. Switch to the alternative.</strong> Assume the alternative value of the parameter is true.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>3. Compute the rejection probability.</strong> Standardize the cutoff under the alternative and read off the area, which is the power.</li>
</ol>

::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
power_overlap(mu0 = 0, mua = 1.1, se0 = 1 / sqrt(10),
              alpha = 0.05, alternative = "greater",
              title = "Power = green area under Hₐ past the cutoff")
```
:::
:::

---

## Example: A Better Espresso Blend

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
A specialty coffee roaster's house espresso has scored a long-run average of **7.0** on a 10-point flavour scale. A new blend is developed, and the roaster will switch only if it truly scores higher. If the new blend's true mean score is $\mu=8.1$, will a 5% test reliably detect the improvement?

A panel of $n=10$ trained graders scores the new blend; from years of calibration, grader scores have $\sigma=1$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
$\sigma$ is known $\Rightarrow$ one-sample $z$ test, reference [$N(0,1)$.]{.nw}
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">Set-up</span>

$$H_0:\mu = 7 \qquad H_a:\mu>7$$

- $n = 10,\quad \sigma = 1,\quad \alpha = 0.05$
- Detect the alternative $\mu = 8.1$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Espresso: Cutoff to Power

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Rejection Rule</span>
One-sided $\alpha=0.05$ gives $z_{\text{crit}}=1.645$. On the $\bar{x}$ scale (since $\sigma$ is known):
$$\bar{x}_*=7+1.645\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\approx 7.520 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{reject if } \bar{x}>7.520$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Find the Power</span>
Assume $\mu=8.1$ is true and find $P(\bar{x}>7.520)$:
$$\text{power}=P\!\left(Z>\tfrac{7.520-8.1}{1/\sqrt{10}}\right)=P(Z>-1.83)=\mathbf{0.9664}$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
power_overlap(mu0 = 7, mua = 8.1, se0 = 1 / sqrt(10),
              alpha = 0.05, alternative = "greater", show_beta = TRUE,
              xlab = "mean flavour score  x̄",
              cutoff_label = "cutoff = 7.52",
              power_label = "power = 0.966",
              beta_label = "β = 0.034",
              width = 500, height = 270)
```
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
A **96.6%** chance of correctly detecting $\mu=8.1$. Since power $=1-\beta$, the green and red areas add to 1:
$$\text{power}=1-\beta=1-0.034=0.966$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Espresso Power

```{webr}
n     <- 10
sigma <- 1
mu0   <- 7
mua   <- 8.1
alpha <- 0.05

# Step 1: cutoff on the xbar scale, under H0
xcrit <- mu0 + qnorm(1 - alpha) * sigma / sqrt(n)

# Steps 2-3: rejection probability when mu = 8.1 is true
power <- 1 - pnorm((xcrit - mua) / (sigma / sqrt(n)))

xcrit
power
```

---

## Visualizing Power: The Power Curve

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
Power is not a single number, it is a **function** of the true mean. Plotting power against $\mu$ gives the **power curve**.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Read it like this</span>

- Near $\mu_0$, power is close to $\alpha$ (hard to detect tiny effects).
- As the true $\mu$ moves away from $\mu_0$, power climbs toward 1.
- The orange dots mark $\mu=7.52$ (power $\approx 0.5$) and $\mu=8.1$ (power $\approx 0.97$).
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
power_curve(mu0 = 7, se = 1 / sqrt(10), alpha = 0.05,
            alternative = "greater", mu_lo = 7, mu_hi = 10,
            marks = c(7.52, 8.1),
            title = "Power vs true mean μ")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

On the power curve for a one-sided test, what happens to the power as the true mean moves farther away from the null value (in the direction of $H_a$)?
::::

- It decreases toward $0$
- [It increases toward $1$]{.correct data-explanation="The farther the truth lies from H₀, the larger the effect and the easier it is to detect, so power rises toward 1. When the true mean sits right at the null value, the power is only about α."}
- It stays constant at $\alpha$
- It is always equal to $\beta$

---

## Example: Under-Dosed Medicine Vials

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card}
A pharmaceutical filling machine should dispense $\mu_0=300$ mg of active drug per vial, with **known** $\sigma=3$ mg from the validated assay. A routine quality check tests only $n=6$ vials — will a 5% test catch a machine that has drifted to a true mean of $\mu=299$ mg?
$$H_0:\mu = 300 \qquad H_a:\mu<300 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
$$\bar{x}_*=300-1.645\cdot\tfrac{3}{\sqrt6}=297.985 \quad(\text{reject if } \bar{x}<297.985)$$
$$\text{power}=P\!\left(Z<\frac{297.985-299}{3/\sqrt6}\right)=P(Z<-0.83)=\mathbf{0.2033}$$
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
Only **20%** power. With just 6 vials, this check will usually **miss** an under-dosing machine — the sample is too small.
:::
:::

---

## Check in R: Vial Power

```{webr}
n <- 6; sigma <- 3; mu0 <- 300; mua <- 299; alpha <- 0.05

xcrit <- mu0 - qnorm(1 - alpha) * sigma / sqrt(n)   # left-tailed cutoff
power <- pnorm((xcrit - mua) / (sigma / sqrt(n)))

c(xcrit = xcrit, power = power)
```

::: {.notebox .fragment}
Try bumping `n` to 30 or 60 and re-run, then watch the power climb as the standard error shrinks.
:::

---

## Interactive: Watch Power Climb with $n$ {.compact}

Use the dropdown to change the sample size for the vial check ($\mu_0=300$, $\mu_a=299$, $\sigma=3$, left-tailed $\alpha=0.05$). As $n$ grows, both curves sharpen, they separate more cleanly, and the green **power** area past the cutoff expands.

:::{style="max-width:840px; margin:0 auto;"}
```{r}
explore_power_n(mu0 = 300, mua = 299, sigma = 3,
                ns = c(6, 15, 30, 60), alpha = 0.05,
                alternative = "less")
```
:::

::: {.thinkbox}
Same 1 mg shortfall, same $\alpha$, only $n$ changes: power rises from $\approx 0.20$ at $n=6$ to $\approx 0.83$ at $n=60$. That is why sample size is your main planning lever.
:::

---

## Interactive: Change Everything {.compact}

Choose the direction of $H_a$, then drag $\mu_0$, $\mu_a$, $\sigma$, and $n$ ($\alpha$ stays at $0.05$) and watch the cutoff, $\beta$, and power react.

:::: {.power-lab}
::: {.col}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof alt = Inputs.select(
  new Map([["μ > μ₀ (greater)", "greater"],
           ["μ < μ₀ (less)", "less"],
           ["μ ≠ μ₀ (two-sided)", "two.sided"]]),
  {value: "greater", label: "Hₐ"}
)
viewof mu0 = Inputs.range([5, 15], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "μ₀"})
viewof mua = Inputs.range([5, 15], {value: 12, step: 0.5, label: "μₐ"})
viewof sigma = Inputs.range([1, 4], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "σ"})
viewof n = Inputs.range([2, 60], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "n"})
```
:::

::: {.col}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
res = {
  const pnorm = (z) => {
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(z));
    const d = Math.exp(-z * z / 2) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI);
    const p = d * t * (0.319381530 + t * (-0.356563782 + t * (1.781477937 +
              t * (-1.821255978 + t * 1.330274429))));
    return z >= 0 ? 1 - p : p;
  };
  const se = sigma / Math.sqrt(n);
  let cuts, inReject, pow;
  if (alt === "greater") {
    cuts = [mu0 + 1.6449 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x > cuts[0];
    pow = 1 - pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se);
  } else if (alt === "less") {
    cuts = [mu0 - 1.6449 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x < cuts[0];
    pow = pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se);
  } else {
    cuts = [mu0 - 1.96 * se, mu0 + 1.96 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x < cuts[0] || x > cuts[1];
    pow = pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se) + 1 - pnorm((cuts[1] - mua) / se);
  }
  const lo = Math.min(mu0, mua) - 4.2 * se;
  const hi = Math.max(mu0, mua) + 4.2 * se;
  const dnorm = (x, m) => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m) / se) ** 2) / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  const data = d3.range(lo, hi, (hi - lo) / 500).map((x) =>
    ({x, h0: dnorm(x, mu0), ha: dnorm(x, mua)}));
  return {se, cuts, inReject, pow, data};
}

html`<div class="power-plot-row">

                            fill: "rgba(46,125,50,0.40)"}),
```

## Example: Monitoring a Server Room

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
A data centre keeps its server hall at $\mu_0=22$°C. Too **hot** and the servers overheat and fail; too **cold** and the cooling bill climbs for no benefit. Each day the monitoring system samples $n=16$ sensor readings; from the sensors' calibration, $\sigma=2$°C. If the cooling has truly drifted to $\mu=23$°C, how likely is the daily check to flag it?
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
A shift in **either** direction matters $\Rightarrow$ two-sided test: $\alpha$ splits into two tails of $\alpha/2=0.025$ each, so $z_{\alpha/2}=1.96$ and there are **two** cutoffs.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">Set-up</span>

$$H_0:\mu = 22 \qquad H_a:\mu \neq 22$$

- $n = 16,\quad \sigma = 2,\quad \alpha = 0.05$
- Detect the alternative $\mu = 23$
- $\sigma$ known $\Rightarrow$ one-sample $z$ test
:::
:::
::::

---

## Two-Sided: Two Cutoffs, Two Power Pieces {.compact}

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Rejection Rule</span>
Two cutoffs, using $z_{\alpha/2}=1.96$:
$$\bar{x}_*=22 \pm 1.96\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{16}} = 22 \pm 0.98$$
$$\text{reject if } \bar{x}<21.02 \;\text{ or }\; \bar{x}>22.98$$
:::

::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Find the Power</span>
Assume $\mu=23$ is true; add the two rejection pieces:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{power} &= P(\bar{x}<21.02)+P(\bar{x}>22.98)\\
&= P(Z<-3.96)+P(Z>-0.04)\\
&\approx 0.000+0.516=\mathbf{0.516}
\end{aligned}$$
:::
::::

::: {style="max-width:900px; margin:0 auto;"}
```{r}
power_two_sided(mu0 = 22, mua = 23, se = 2 / sqrt(16), alpha = 0.05,
                xlab = "mean server-hall temperature  x̄")
```
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Nearly all the power comes from the rejection tail **nearest** the true mean — the far tail adds $\approx 0$. Even so, a full 1°C drift is caught only about half the time.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

The vial check has only 20% power against $\mu=299$. Which single change raises power the **most** without touching $\alpha$ or the true process?
::::

- Use a smaller sample to save money
- [Increase the sample size $n$]{.correct data-explanation="Larger n shrinks the standard error σ/√n, narrowing both sampling distributions, shrinking β and raising power. α and the true mean are held fixed."}
- Re-label the hypotheses
- Hope the next sample looks different

---

## 7.3 Using Power to Determine Sample Size

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Too small</span>
Low power - real, meaningful effects slip through undetected. The study is wasted.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Too large</span>
Wasteful - extra time, cost, and participants for precision you did not need.
:::
::::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Power analysis finds the **minimum $n$** that detects an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power), while holding the Type I rate at $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
To run it you must supply three ingredients: the standard deviation $\sigma$, the significance level $\alpha$, and the effect size $\mu_0-\mu_a$ you want to detect.
:::

---

## The Sample-Size Idea

::: {.slide-stack}
<ol class="step-list spaced-steps">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>1. Cutoff from $H_0$.</strong> The cutoff $\bar{x}_*$ is the borderline value of the sample mean that decides whether you reject $H_0$ or not. Write it using the null mean and the critical value $z_\alpha$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>2. Cutoff from the target power.</strong> Write the same $\bar{x}_*$ using the alternative mean and $z_\beta$ (the $z$ giving the desired power).</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>3. Set the two expressions equal and solve for $n$.</strong> Round <em>up</em> to the next whole observation.</li>
</ol>

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">One-sided sample-size formula</span>
$$n=\left(\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\mu_0-\mu_a}\right)^{2}$$
where $z_\beta$ is the standard-normal value matching the target power.
:::
:::

---

## Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card}
A product team's app currently averages $\mu_0=100$ daily active minutes. A new onboarding flow is believed to lift engagement. With $\sigma=14$, they want **power $0.60$** to detect a true mean of $\mu=103$. What is the smallest $n$?
$$H_0:\mu=100 \qquad H_a:\mu>100 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Cutoff under $H_0$</span> $\;\bar{x}_*=100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}$

<span class="label">Cutoff for power 0.60</span> $\;P(Z>-0.25)\approx 0.60 \;\Rightarrow\; \bar{x}_*=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}$

<span class="label">Equate and solve</span>
$$100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}
\;\Rightarrow\; n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.25)\cdot 14}{103-100}\right)^2\approx 78.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=79}$$
:::
:::

---

## Check in R: Sample Size for the Lift

```{webr}
mu0 <- 100; mua <- 103; sigma <- 14; alpha <- 0.05; power <- 0.60

z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
z_beta  <- qnorm(power)

n <- ((z_alpha + z_beta) * sigma / (mua - mu0))^2
ceiling(n)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
$n\approx 78.2$, so a minimum of **79** observations guarantees power of at least 0.60. (Using the rounded $z_\beta=0.25$ from the table gives the same answer.)
:::

---

## Example: Vending-Machine Coffee

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card}
A campus vending machine advertises $225$ ml cups ($\sigma=7$ ml). You suspect it pours **less**. How many cups must you sample to reach **power $0.80$** against a true mean of $\mu=223$ ml? (Target: $P(Z<0.84)\approx0.80$, so $z_\beta=0.84$.)
$$H_0:\mu=225 \qquad H_a:\mu<225 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Equate the two cutoffs</span> $\;225-1.645\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}=223+0.84\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}$

<span class="label">Solve for $n$</span>
$$n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.84)\cdot 7}{225-223}\right)^2\approx 75.6 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=76}$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
A minimum of **76 cups** delivers the desired 0.80 power against a 2 ml shortfall.
:::
:::

---

## Check in R: Coffee Sample Size

```{webr}
mu0 <- 225; mua <- 223; sigma <- 7; alpha <- 0.05; power <- 0.80

z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
z_beta  <- qnorm(power)

n <- ((z_alpha + z_beta) * sigma / (mu0 - mua))^2
ceiling(n)
```

::: {.notebox .fragment}
`power.t.test` and `power.prop.test` automate these calculations once you know $\sigma$, $\alpha$, the effect size, and the target power.
:::

---

## Power for a Proportion: Same Logic

::: {.defbox}
For a one-sided test of $p$, the rejection cutoff uses the **null** standard error, but power is computed with the **alternative** standard error:

$$\hat p^{\,*}=p_0 \mathbin{\substack{+\\[-4pt]-}} z_\alpha\sqrt{\tfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}, \qquad
\text{power}=P\!\left(\hat p \text{ in reject region}\;\middle|\; p=p_a\right)$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Which sign on $z_\alpha$?</span>

| Test | Cutoff $\hat p^{\,*}$ | Reject when |
|---|---|---|
| $H_a:p<p_0$ | $p_0-z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$ | $\hat p<\hat p^{\,*}$ |
| $H_a:p>p_0$ | $p_0+z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$ | $\hat p>\hat p^{\,*}$ |
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Three steps, same as the mean</span>

- Find the cutoff $\hat p^{\,*}$ from $p_0$ and $z_\alpha$.
- Standardize that cutoff under $p=p_a$ using $\text{SE}_a$.
- The tail area past it is the power.
:::

---

## A Streaming Proportion Test

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card}
A streaming platform claims $90\%$ of viewers finish episode 1. Researchers suspect **fewer** do, and test $H_0:p=0.90$ vs $H_a:p<0.90$ at $\alpha=0.05$. The truth is $p=0.85$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">The question</span>
How does the power to detect this 5-point drop change as the sample grows from $n=50$ to $n=200$?
:::
:::

---

## Streaming Example: Power Grows with $n$

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
| $n$ | cutoff $\hat p^{\,*}$ | $z$ under $p=0.85$ | Power |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | 0.8302 | $-0.39$ | 0.347 |
| 100 | 0.8507 | $0.02$ | 0.507 |
| 200 | 0.8651 | $0.60$ | 0.725 |

::: {.thinkbox .table-note}
Same effect (a drop from 0.90 to 0.85), same $\alpha$, only $n$ changes. Power climbs from 35% to 73%.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
prop_power_n(p0 = 0.90, pa = 0.85, alpha = 0.05, alternative = "less",
             n_lo = 20, n_hi = 400, marks = c(50, 100, 200),
             title = "Power vs n (p₀ = 0.90, true p = 0.85)")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Proportion Power

```{webr}
p0 <- 0.90; pa <- 0.85; alpha <- 0.05

prop_power <- function(n) {
  se0   <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)   # null SE for the cutoff
  sea   <- sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / n)   # alternative SE for the power
  pcrit <- p0 - qnorm(1 - alpha) * se0
  pnorm((pcrit - pa) / sea)
}

sapply(c(50, 100, 200), prop_power)
```

---

## How Many Viewers for Power 0.80?

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card}
Keep $H_0:p=0.90$, $H_a:p<0.90$, true $p=0.85$, $\alpha=0.05$. Set power $=0.80$ ($z_\beta=0.8416$) and equate the two cutoff expressions:
$$0.90-1.645\sqrt{\tfrac{0.90(0.10)}{n}}=0.85+0.8416\sqrt{\tfrac{0.85(0.15)}{n}}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
$$\sqrt n=\frac{1.645\sqrt{0.09}+0.8416\sqrt{0.1275}}{0.05}=\frac{0.4935+0.3005}{0.05}\approx 15.88$$
$$n\approx 252.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=253}$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Detecting a modest 5-point drop with 80% power takes **253 viewers**, far more than the 50-200 above. Smaller effects always demand larger samples.
:::
:::

---

## General Power Formulas

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Right-tailed, $H_a:\mu>\mu_0$</span>
$$\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\ge z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]$$
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Left-tailed, $H_a:\mu<\mu_0$</span>
$$\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\le -z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]$$
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two-sided, $H_a:\mu\ne\mu_0$</span>
$$\text{Power}(\mu_a)=1-P\!\left[-z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]$$
:::
:::

---

## What You Need to Know

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Standard deviation</span>
$\sigma$ - the spread of the variable being measured.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Significance level</span>
$\alpha$ - the fixed Type I error rate you are willing to tolerate.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Effect size</span>
$\mu_0-\mu_a$ - the smallest difference worth detecting.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
With data in hand it is more common to report a **p-value** than a fixed reject/not-reject decision: it measures the strength of evidence against $H_0$ and leaves the action up to each reader.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

You want to detect a *smaller* effect than originally planned, keeping $\alpha$, $\sigma$, and power the same. What happens to the required sample size?
::::

- It decreases
- It stays the same
- [It increases]{.correct data-explanation="In n = ((zα+zβ)σ / (μ0−μa))², the effect size μ0−μa is in the denominator. A smaller effect means a smaller denominator, so n grows, and smaller effects need larger samples."}
- It becomes undefined

---

## Chapter 7 Cheat Sheet

| Quantity | Formula / idea |
|---|---|
| Power | $1-\beta=P(\text{reject } H_0\mid H_0 \text{ false})$ |
| Type I error | $\alpha=P(\text{reject } H_0\mid H_0 \text{ true})$ |
| Type II error | $\beta=P(\text{fail to reject}\mid H_0 \text{ false})$ |
| Cutoff (right-tailed) | $\bar{x}_*=\mu_0+z_\alpha\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ |
| Power (right-tailed) | $P\!\big(Z\ge z_\alpha+\sqrt n(\mu_0-\mu_a)/\sigma\big)$ |
| Sample size (one-sided) | $n=\big((z_\alpha+z_\beta)\sigma/(\mu_0-\mu_a)\big)^2$ |

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .spaced-note}
Always round a computed sample size **up** to the next whole observation so the achieved power is at least the target.
:::

::: {.examplebox}
**Chapter 8 - Analysis of Variance**

We extend hypothesis testing from one or two groups to **several** group means at once, using the $F$-distribution to ask whether any of the group means differ.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One-slide takeaway.** Power $=1-\beta$ is a test's ability to detect a real effect. It rises with effect size, sample size, and $\alpha$, and falls with variability, so planning $n$ in advance is how we guarantee a study can succeed.
:::
